h1: Watts to Amps Calculator for DC, Single-Phase and Three-Phase
author: ali-ahmad

fields.name: watts
fields.label: Power
fields.hint: Watts from the appliance label, or the total of several appliances. For kW, multiply by 1,000.

fields.name: mode
fields.label: Supply type
fields.hint: DC ignores power factor. Three-phase uses the line-to-line voltage and the square root of three.

fields.name: volts
fields.label: Voltage
fields.hint: Leave blank for standard mains: 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase. For DC enter the battery voltage (12, 24, 48). For the US enter 120.

fields.name: pf
fields.label: Power factor
fields.hint: 1 for heaters, kettles, irons and bulbs; about 0.8 for motors, ACs, fridges and mixed loads. Ignored for DC.

answer: {{in.watts|int}} watts is {{out.amps|2}} amps on a {{in.volts|int}} V single-phase supply at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}, or {{ex.0.out.amps|2}} A for a heater with a power factor of one. Amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor); for DC the power factor is one, and for three-phase the volts are multiplied by the square root of three.
how: {{in.watts}} W ÷ ({{out.k|4}} × {{out.volts}} V × {{out.pf|2}} power factor) = {{out.amps|2}} A. The first factor is one for DC and single-phase and √3 for three-phase, where the volts are the line-to-line voltage and the result is the current in each line. On DC the power factor is always one, so amps are simply watts ÷ volts.
key_facts: Amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor). On a {{in.volts|int}} V single-phase supply, {{in.watts|int}} W at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}} draws {{out.amps|2}} A.

Watts alone do not give amps: the same {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W draws {{ex.1.out.amps|2}} A from a {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V battery but only {{ex.4.out.amps|2}} A at {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V mains with a power factor of one.

At {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} V (US and Canada) a {{ex.3.in.watts|int}} W heater draws {{ex.3.out.amps|2}} A, close to twice the {{ex.0.out.amps|2}} A the same heater draws on a {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V supply.
On three-phase {{ex.2.out.volts|int}} V, {{ex.2.in.watts|int}} W at a power factor of {{ex.2.in.pf|2}} draws {{ex.2.out.amps|2}} A in each line wire.

formula.text: DC: I = P ÷ V;  single-phase AC: I = P ÷ (V × PF);  three-phase AC: I = P ÷ (√3 × V × PF)
lines: P = real power in watts (W); for kW multiply by 1,000
V = voltage: the battery voltage for DC, phase-to-neutral for single-phase, line-to-line for three-phase
PF = power factor between 0 and 1 (1 for heating loads)

p: On a {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V home supply, {{ex.0.in.watts|int}} W is {{ex.0.out.amps|2}} A for a heater, kettle or iron (power factor one) and {{out.amps|2}} A for a motor or AC at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}. The watts are the same; the motor draws more current because part of it flows back and forth without doing work.
On a {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} V US supply the same heater draws {{ex.3.out.amps|2}} A, close to twice as much current, so always enter the voltage of the supply the load actually runs on.

sections.h2: Is {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} watts one amp? How many watts per amp?
p: No. A watt is power, an amp is current, and the voltage links them. {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W is {{ex.1.out.amps|2}} A from a {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V battery but {{ex.4.out.amps|2}} A from {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V mains. The higher the voltage, the fewer amps for the same watts.

Each amp carries as many watts as the voltage times the power factor: on {{d.v_1ph|int}} V mains with a power factor of one, one amp is {{d.v_1ph|int}} W. The amps to watts calculator does that direction.

sections.h2: Watts, amps and volts: how they relate
p: Power is voltage times current. On DC that is the whole story: watts = volts × amps. On AC the current and voltage are slightly out of step in motors, compressors and electronics, so a power factor below one is added: watts = volts × amps × power factor.

Three-phase supplies use three live wires. The power is shared between them, so the formula uses the square root of three and the line-to-line voltage ({{d.v_3ph|int}} V in Pakistan), and the result is the current in each line.

sections.h2: DC watts to amps: batteries, solar and cars
p: Choose DC and enter the battery voltage. A {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W load on a {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V battery draws {{ex.1.out.amps|2}} A, which is why low-voltage inverters need thick cables. On a battery inverter, add the inverter's losses to the watts first; the 12V watts to amps calculator does this for you.

examples.title: What is {{in.watts|int}} W in amps on a {{in.volts|int}} V supply?
examples.text: {{in.watts|int}} W ÷ ({{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|int}}) = {{out.amps|2}} A for a heater or kettle. A motor of the same watts at a power factor below one draws more.

examples.title: {{in.watts|int}} W from a {{in.volts|int}} V battery (DC)
examples.text: {{in.watts|int}} W ÷ {{in.volts|int}} V = {{out.amps|2}} A. DC has no power factor, so this is the current the battery and its cable must carry, before inverter losses.

examples.title: {{in.watts|int}} W on three-phase {{out.volts|int}} V
examples.text: {{in.watts|int}} W ÷ (√3 × {{out.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|2}}) = {{out.amps|2}} A in each line. The voltage box was left blank, so the calculator used the standard three-phase line-to-line voltage.

examples.title: {{in.watts|int}} W heater at {{in.volts|int}} V (US and Canada)
examples.text: {{in.watts|int}} W ÷ ({{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|int}}) = {{out.amps|2}} A. A lower voltage means more amps for the same watts.

examples.title: How many amps is {{in.watts|int}} watts at {{in.volts|int}} V?
examples.text: {{in.watts|int}} W ÷ ({{in.volts|int}} V × {{in.pf|int}}) = {{out.amps|2}} A for a resistive load such as an iron or water heater.

mistakes: Dividing watts by volts for an AC, fridge or water motor. Their power factor is below one, so the real current is higher; use about {{d.pf_mixed|2}} unless the label says otherwise.
Using {{d.v_1ph|int}} V in the three-phase formula. Three-phase needs the line-to-line voltage ({{d.v_3ph|int}} V) together with the square root of three.
Forgetting that DC current is large at low voltage. A load that draws a few amps from the mains can draw tens of amps from a battery, and the cable must be sized for that.
Treating the calculated amps as the breaker or wire size. Cables and breakers need a margin above the running current; the breaker size calculator adds it.
safety: The current from this page is a starting point for choosing cable and breakers, not the final choice. Use the wire size and breaker size calculators for the margins and voltage drop, and have a licensed electrician connect any new circuit.

faq.a: {{ex.4.out.amps|2}} A on a {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V single-phase supply with a power factor of one. From a {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V battery the same {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W draws {{ex.1.out.amps|2}} A, because current depends on the voltage.
{{ex.0.out.amps|2}} A at {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V for a heating load, and {{out.amps|2}} A at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}} for a motor or mixed load.

faq.q: How many amps does a {{ex.3.in.watts|int}} W heater draw at {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} V?
faq.a: {{ex.3.out.amps|2}} A at {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} V, against {{ex.0.out.amps|2}} A on a {{ex.0.in.volts|int}} V supply. Roughly halving the voltage roughly doubles the current, which is why US heaters need heavier cable.

faq.q: What is the watts to amps formula?
faq.a: Amps = watts ÷ volts for DC; amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor) for single-phase AC; amps = watts ÷ (√3 × line-to-line volts × power factor) for three-phase.
No. Watts measure power and amps measure current. {{ex.1.in.watts|int}} W is {{ex.4.out.amps|2}} A on {{ex.4.in.volts|int}} V mains and {{ex.1.out.amps|2}} A from a {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V battery.

Watts per amp equals the voltage times the power factor. On {{d.v_1ph|int}} V mains with a power factor of one, each amp carries {{d.v_1ph|int}} W; on a {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} V battery each amp carries only {{ex.1.in.volts|int}} W.

faq.q: How do I convert watts to amps on three-phase?
faq.a: Divide the watts by √3 × the line-to-line voltage × the power factor. {{ex.2.in.watts|int}} W at {{ex.2.out.volts|int}} V and a power factor of {{ex.2.in.pf|2}} is {{ex.2.out.amps|2}} A per line. The 3 phase amps calculator also handles kW and kVA ratings.
